### What is plugged in {#sec-plugin-targets}

| Scale | Plug-in estimator | Source | Methods |
|---|---|---|---|
| Technical size factor $s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c$, extrinsic noise $\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}$ | [the Poisson-gene size factor](theory-review-distribution-aware-deconvolution.html#eq-poisson-size-factor) on Poisson genes; spike-ins | reference cells | Fang and Pachter; [the denoised within-type covariance](theory-review-distribution-aware-deconvolution.html#eq-denoised-within) |
| Cell size $S_j$ | mean UMI total per type; CLTS; RNA-content assay | reference, or external assay | `MuSiC`, `ReDeconv`, `EPIC`, `quanTIseq` |
| Reference scale $a^{\mathrm{ref}}_r$ | grand mean of the reference matrix | reference alone | `MEAD` ($\hat\gamma_j$) |
| Gene-wise platform ratio $\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$ | regression on paired samples; moment matching; pseudo-bulk MLE | paired cohort, or all bulks | `Bisque`, `RCTD` stage 1 |
| Sample scale $c_i$ | observed library size as an offset | bulk total | `RCTD` ($N_i$) |
| Type moments $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}$, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ | reference averages and covariances | reference | every method except `RNA-Sieve` and `MEAD` |

: Quantities that the reviewed methods estimate before the deconvolution and then hold fixed. {#tbl-plugin-targets}

With the plug-ins, the bulk law of Strategy 2 becomes

$$
\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i};\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}
\sim\mathcal{N}_G\Bigl(
\hat c_i\,\hat{\tilde{\mathbf{B}}}\sum_jp_{ji}\hat S_j\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\cdot j},\;
\hat{\tilde{\mathbf{B}}}\bigl[\hat c_i^{2}\boldsymbol{S}_B(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})+\hat\phi_i\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})\bigr]\hat{\tilde{\mathbf{B}}}
+\boldsymbol{D}_i\Bigr),
$$ {#eq-plugin-law}

with $\hat{\tilde{\mathbf{B}}}=\operatorname{diag}(\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}})$, plugged-in
sizes $\hat S_j$ and relative abundances $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\cdot j}$, and
$\boldsymbol{S}_W$ built from [the denoised within-type covariance](theory-review-distribution-aware-deconvolution.html#eq-denoised-within). The tuple of
@thm-score-general is that of @sec-av-replicates with
$\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}$ replaced by $\hat c_i\hat{\tilde{\mathbf{B}}}\hat S_j\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\cdot j}$
and every covariance block sandwiched by $\hat{\tilde{\mathbf{B}}}$;
only $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$ (and, if kept free, $\boldsymbol{\tau}^{2}$)
remains in the score.

### Why plug in: identifiability {#sec-plugin-identifiability}

Some scales are not identified from the bulk sample at all, so a
plug-in is not a convenience but the only route.

- **Cell size and composition.** Only $p_{ji}S_j$ enters the mean
  (@eq-music-mean). Fitting with a wrong $\hat S_j$ makes the estimator
  converge to $\tilde p_{ji}\propto p_{ji}S_j/\hat S_j$: the cell
  fractions are rescaled by the ratio of true to plugged-in sizes. That
  is `MEAD`'s cell-size rescaling and `MuSiC`'s assumption A3$'$.
- **Gene-wise platform and composition.** A free $\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$ fitted on
  the sample being deconvolved absorbs any residual, and with perfect
  markers it absorbs a type-specific factor (`MEAD`, Theorem 1). `RCTD`
  and `Bisque` estimate it on all bulks or on a paired cohort; `MEAD`
  declines to estimate it and treats it as noise.
- **Technical versus biological size factors.** One cell's counts
  identify only the product $s^{\mathrm{bio}}_cs^{\mathrm{tech}}_c$;
  spike-ins or ambient RNA separate them
  [@fangExtrinsicBiologicalStochasticity2025].

### What plugging in costs: uncertainty {#sec-plugin-uncertainty}

Holding $\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}$ fixed treats it as exact. Let
$\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$ solve the bulk score
$\boldsymbol{U}(\boldsymbol{p};\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}})=\boldsymbol{0}$, with
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}$ estimated from independent auxiliary data with
covariance $\boldsymbol{V}_{\eta}$. A first-order expansion in both
arguments (the standard two-step M-estimation argument) gives

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})
\approx I_{pp}^{-1}+I_{pp}^{-1}I_{p\eta}\,\boldsymbol{V}_{\eta}\,I_{\eta p}I_{pp}^{-1},
$$ {#eq-plugin-variance}

with the blocks of @eq-schur-information. The naive plug-in variance
$I_{pp}^{-1}$ omits the second term and under-covers whenever the cross
block $I_{p\eta}$ is non-zero; `MuSiC` and `DECALS` treat the reference
means as exact in that sense, whereas `RNA-Sieve` and `MEAD` propagate
reference noise. Compare with joint estimation. By the Woodbury
identity,

$$
I_{p\mid\eta}^{-1}
=I_{pp}^{-1}+I_{pp}^{-1}I_{p\eta}\bigl(I_{\eta\eta}-I_{\eta p}I_{pp}^{-1}I_{p\eta}\bigr)^{-1}I_{\eta p}I_{pp}^{-1},
$$ {#eq-joint-woodbury}

so joint estimation is @eq-plugin-variance with
$\boldsymbol{V}_{\eta}$ equal to the variance of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}$
estimated from the bulk itself. The comparison is therefore explicit:
a plug-in is more precise than joint estimation exactly when the
auxiliary data know the scale better than the bulk does, and it is
biased, not merely noisier, when the auxiliary data measure a
different scale (another protocol, another tissue, another
condition).

### Affine platform maps {#sec-persp-affine}

@sec-cc-scale used one scalar $a_i$. Capture efficiency in
single-cell protocols is gene dependent and technology dependent, so
the alignment between reference and bulk is in general an affine
map. Let $\boldsymbol{o}\in\mathbb{R}^{G}$ be a background intercept and
$\tilde{\mathbf{B}}_j=\operatorname{diag}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}_j)$ a gene-wise,
type-wise platform ratio that also carries the sample scale. Affine
invariance of the Gaussian family gives exactly

$$
\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}
=\boldsymbol{o}+\sum_j\tilde{\mathbf{B}}_j\boldsymbol{T}_{ji}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i
\sim\mathcal{N}_G\Bigl(
\boldsymbol{o}+\sum_jm_{ji}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}_j\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\;
\sum_jm_{ji}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}_j\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}_j+\boldsymbol{D}_i
\Bigr),
$$ {#eq-persp-affine}

and the tuple of @thm-score-general follows by replacing
$\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}$ with $\tilde{\mathbf{B}}_j\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}$ and
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ with $\tilde{\mathbf{B}}_j\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}_j$.
Three special cases are already in the literature.
$\tilde{\mathbf{B}}_j=a_i\mathbf{I}_G$, $\boldsymbol{o}=\boldsymbol{0}$ is
@sec-cc-scale. A gene- and subject-specific intercept $\boldsymbol{o}$ with
$\tilde{\mathbf{B}}_j=\mathbf{I}_G$ is what `MuSiC` adds to its equation (8)
to absorb protocol bias [@wangBulkTissueCell2019].
$\tilde{\mathbf{B}}_j=\tilde{\mathbf{B}}$ shared across types, with a per-gene
intercept, is the `Bisque` transformation learned on paired
individuals [@jewAccurateEstimationCell2020] and the platform ratio of
`MEAD` and `RCTD` (@sec-alignment).

Two warnings carry over. A free $\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$ fitted on the sample
being deconvolved is not identified from $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$; it
must come from a paired cohort, a pseudo-bulk of all samples, or an
external measurement model of the capture probabilities $b_g$ of
both protocols [@sarkarSeparatingMeasurementExpression2021]. A
type-wise $\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}_j$ is weaker still, and a candidate only
when sorted bulk profiles of type $j$ exist on the bulk platform. Any
such plug-in is protocol specific, so $\tilde{\mathbf{B}}_j$ and $S_j$ are
stored with the reference, never re-estimated per bulk sample; the
measurement-model estimates of $S_j$ are in @sec-uncoupling.

# RNA fraction versus cell fraction {#sec-uncoupling}

A linear engine fitted on a library-normalised signature
$\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}$, or on a normalised bulk, estimates the
**RNA mass fraction** $\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}$, not the cytometric cell
fraction $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$, unless transcriptome sizes $S_j$ (mean
transcripts per cell; @nte-notation) are homogeneous. Fitted on the
raw per-cell means $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}$, it returns
$\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$ directly, provided their UMI totals $S_j$ reflect
RNA content. With $\hat q_{j}$ an RNA-scale estimate,

$$
\hat p_{j}
=\frac{\hat q_{j}/S_{j}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{J}\hat q_{\ell}/S_{\ell}}.
$$ {#eq-rna-to-cell}

**Post-correction** treats $S_j$ as measured (or proxied). `EPIC` and
`quanTIseq` rescale $\hat{\boldsymbol{q}}$ using kit-based mRNA content or
housekeeping-gene / proteasome-subunit surrogates
[@racleSimultaneousEnumerationCancer2017; @finotello_etal19]. `MuSiC`
uses average cell-type library size as a size proxy and warns that TPM
can discard the information needed to recover cell fractions
[@wangBulkTissueCell2019]. `ReDeconv` separates global library-size
normalisation from cell-type transcriptome size
[@luTranscriptomeSizeMatters2025].

**Joint estimation** treats $S_j$ as unknown. `MMAD` estimates
extraction efficiencies by non-linear conjugate gradients, so the
mixture is no longer linear
[@liebnerMMADMicroarrayMicrodissection2014]. A DeCovarT analogue would
introduce $S_j$ inside the mean
$\sum_{j}p_{ji}S_{j}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}$ (with a product-simplex
constraint on $(p_{j}S_{j})$), rather than assuming $S_j$ known.
If $S_j$ is observed, plug it in. Do not estimate a free gene-wise
platform ratio $\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$ in the same fit (@sec-alignment).

**Bayesian transcript totals.** With no RNA-content assay and no
cytometry ground truth, $S_j$ has to come from a measurement model on
the single-cell counts. `bayNorm` takes the observed count of gene $g$
in cell $c$ as a binomial draw from an unobserved original count, with
cell-specific capture efficiency $b_c$, and a negative binomial prior
fit by empirical Bayes
[@tangBayNormBayesianGene2020]. The posterior is a shifted negative
binomial for that original count. Summing the posterior means over
genes is that cell's inferred transcript total. $S_j$ is the mean of
those totals inside type $j$. A single mean capture efficiency scales
every cell, so it cancels in the ratios of @eq-rna-to-cell; the
absolute molecule number still needs an external anchor (the paper uses
smFISH for that check). `Sanity` is the expression-model counterpart
of the split in [measurement and expression models](theory-review-distribution-aware-deconvolution.html#sec-measurement): a Poisson measurement
model and a prior on the expression state, with the posterior reported as a
denoised activity and an error bar, not as a molecule count
[@bredaBayesianInferenceGene2021]. Use the `bayNorm` total as $S_j$.
Use `Sanity` when $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}$ itself must be corrected
for sampling noise before it enters the `MuSiC` mean, @eq-music-mean. The observed
library size is a capture total, not this $S_j$.

# Cell size in the mean and in the covariance {#sec-cell-size-covariance}

Write a type-$j$ cell as $\boldsymbol{x}=S_j\boldsymbol{u}$, with $S_j$ its
transcriptome size and $\boldsymbol{u}$ its relative expression:
$\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{u}]=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}$,
$\mathbf{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}=1$ and
$\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{u})=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\theta}_j$. A cell $S_j$
times larger is $S_j$ times larger in every gene, so its size enters the
mean linearly and the covariance quadratically:

$$
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}=S_j\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}=S_j^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\theta}_j .
$$ {#eq-cell-size-moments}

These are the moments of the cellular fit
(`reference = "cellular_raw"` in
[`rescale_single_cell_moments()`](../reference/rescale_single_cell_moments.html)).
Plugged into @eq-av-scale-law they make $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$ the cell
fractions.

The transcript-fraction fit follows from the same cells. The type-$j$
total of sample $i$ has mean $m_{ji}S_j\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}$ and
covariance $m_{ji}S_j^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\theta}_j$. With
$T_i=\sum_\ell m_{\ell i}S_\ell$ transcripts in the sample and
$q_{ji}=m_{ji}S_j/T_i$,

$$
\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}]
=a_iT_i\sum_j q_{ji}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i})
=a_i^{2}T_i\sum_j q_{ji}S_j\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\theta}_j .
$$ {#eq-transcript-moments}

This is the linear mixture of @eq-av-scale-law again, with composition
$\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}$, scales $c_i=a_iT_i$ and $\phi_i=a_i^{2}T_i$, and
reference $(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j},S_j\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\theta}_j)$
(`reference = "transcript_raw"`). The cell size leaves the mean but
stays in the covariance with one power fewer; the fitted transcript
fractions become cell fractions through @eq-rna-to-cell.

Two consequences follow.

- **Types of equal size overlap as their relative profiles do.** The map
  $\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto\boldsymbol{x}/S$ is affine, and the overlap of two
  Gaussians does not change under a common affine map
  ([overlap and total variation](theory-distance-covariance.html#sec-overlap-tv)).
  Two types with the same size $S$ therefore overlap exactly as
  $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\theta}_j)$ and
  $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot\ell},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\theta}_\ell)$ do. When
  the children of a lineage share a cell size, the within-lineage overlap
  does not depend on that size; unequal sizes between lineages move the
  lineages apart and reweight the bulk.
- **Rescaling the mean alone changes the model.** Multiplying the mean by
  $S_j$ while holding $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ fixed makes a larger cell
  relatively less noisy, with a coefficient of variation that falls as
  $1/S_j$. `rescale_single_cell_moments()` scales both moments as in
  @eq-cell-size-moments, so a simulated cell keeps its relative noise when
  its size changes.

# Summary and critical comparison {#sec-summary}

| | Strategy 1: cell counts | Strategy 2: averaged mixture | Strategy 3: compositional | Strategy 4: plug-in scales | Released DeCovarT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Target | $\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i}\in\mathbb{N}^{J}$, then $\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{m}/n$ | $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\in\Delta^{J-1}$, $n_i$ nuisance | RNA fractions $\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}$ | $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$ given $\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}$ | $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\in\Delta^{J-1}$ |
| Covariance weights | linear $m_{ji}$ in $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$; quadratic $m_{ji}^{2}$ in $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j}$ | linear $\phi_ip_{ji}$; quadratic $c_i^{2}p_{ji}^{2}$ | delta-method image of either | as Strategy 2, rescaled by $\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}}$, $\hat c_i$ | quadratic $p_{ji}^{2}$ only |
| Constraint | none; lattice | simplex via ILR | closure, singular | simplex via ILR | simplex via ILR |
| Scale identification | mean fixes $a\boldsymbol{m}$; covariance fixes $a$ | mean fixes $c$; covariance fixes $\phi$ | scale removed | from auxiliary data | $c_i=1$ |
| Reviewed methods | `RNA-Sieve`, `DWLS`, `MuSiC` eq. (2) | `DECALS`, `MEAD`, DeCovarT | `MuSiC`, `Bisque`, `DECALS` | `MuSiC` ($S_j$), `RCTD`, `Bisque`, `MEAD` ($\hat\gamma$) | -- |
| Advantages | counts are the physical quantity; zeros are ordinary points; linear covariance, one Cholesky per iteration | DeCovarT is its noise-free limit; simplex identifies $a$; direct comparison with `DECALS`, `MEAD` | matches CPM/TPM pipelines; no scale to estimate | breaks non-identifiability of $S_j$ and $\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$; uses external information | implemented; exact Gaussian; sparse $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$ as declared input |
| Drawbacks | $a$ needs $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ on the reference molecule scale; integer search for rare types | $\phi$ and $\boldsymbol{D}$ separated only through off-diagonal structure | induced correlations; $\boldsymbol{q}\neq\boldsymbol{p}$ unless $S_j$ constant | biased if the auxiliary scale differs; variance needs @eq-plugin-variance | $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ must be a between-replicate covariance; silences $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ for rare types |

: The four formulations and the released model. {#tbl-strategies}

@tbl-strategies points to Strategy 2, with Strategy 1 as its
count-scale chart. For one UMI donor, one bulk sample and no
covariates, the model kept is its linear layer, @eq-av-scale-law, on
raw per-cell means, with both scales $c_i,\phi_i$ estimated or
profiled and no $\boldsymbol{S}_B$ or $\boldsymbol{D}_i$ layer: $\boldsymbol{S}_B$ needs
$R\ge 2$ donors, and a bulk residual cannot be separated from the
scales without further assumptions. Its quasi-likelihood form and
inference are the
[final choice](theory-population-inference.html#sec-final-choice) of
the inference vignette. With $R\ge 2$ donors the four layers of
@sec-av-replicates apply, with $S_j$ and $\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$ plugged in as
in Strategy 4 and the within-type covariance cleaned as in
[the denoised within-type covariance](theory-review-distribution-aware-deconvolution.html#eq-denoised-within).
Four further alternatives stay inside the multivariate Gaussian regime
and deserve a place in a simulation study before any is implemented.

1. **Errors in variables for the signature.** The reference mean is
   itself an average of $C_j$ cells, so
   $\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}_{\cdot j}\sim\mathcal{N}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}/C_j)$.
   Marginalising it adds $c_i^{2}\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}/C_j$ to
   @eq-av-four-layer: a quadratic within-type term that is Monte Carlo
   error of the signature, not biology, and that vanishes as the
   reference grows. `RNA-Sieve` and `MEAD` carry it
   [@erdmann-phamLikelihoodbasedDeconvolutionBulk2021; @xieStatisticalInferenceCell2026].
   It is the one quadratic term that a one-replicate reference does
   identify.
2. **Residual regression for $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j}$.** When $R=1$ but
   $N\ge J$ bulk samples share the reference, the `DECALS` moment
   regression of residual outer products on $\hat p_{ji}^{2}$
   estimates a between-population covariance without single-cell
   replicates. A diagonal restriction keeps it estimable.
3. **Multi-sample pooling.** Shared $a$ across samples
   (@sec-av-scale), shared $\boldsymbol{D}$ across technical replicates, or
   shared $n$ across samples of the same tissue mass turn weakly
   identified per-sample scalars into pooled ones.
4. **Compositional Gaussian on the bulk side.** If a pipeline insists
   on normalised bulk, model $\operatorname{clr}(\boldsymbol{Z}_i)$ or
   $\operatorname{ilr}(\boldsymbol{Z}_i)$ as Gaussian (a logistic-normal
   bulk) with mean the log-ratio image of the mixture
   [@aitchisonStatisticalAnalysisCompositional1982;
   @pawlowsky-glahnCompositionalDataAnalysis2011]. The mean map is no
   longer linear in $\boldsymbol{p}$, so the analytic score of
   @thm-score-general still applies but $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{kl}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$.

Outside the Gaussian regime, a Poisson–log-normal read-level mixture
(`RCTD`, [`RCTD`](theory-review-distribution-aware-deconvolution.html#sec-rctd)) is the natural competitor.

Strategy 4 is orthogonal to that choice: any of the laws above can be
fitted with plug-in scales. The rule that follows from
@sec-strategy-plugin is to plug in what the bulk cannot identify
($S_j$, $\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$, $s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c$), to estimate jointly what
it identifies well ($c_i$ and $\phi_i$ on the simplex chart), and in both cases to
report @eq-plugin-variance rather than the naive $I_{pp}^{-1}$.

# The implemented fit: profile Newton {#sec-profile-newton}

[`deconvolute_single_cell()`](../reference/deconvolute_single_cell.html)
fits the linear layer of Strategy 2, @eq-av-scale-law, to one bulk
sample and estimates both scales. Intervals for the composition and for
the scales are derived in the
[single-cell inference vignette](theory-single-cell-inference.html).

## Closed-form scales and the profile log-likelihood {#sec-profile-scales}

For one bulk sample, with $\boldsymbol{W}=\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})^{-1}$,
$\boldsymbol{m}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}$ and
$\boldsymbol{r}=\boldsymbol{y}-c\boldsymbol{m}$, the log-likelihood of
@eq-av-scale-law is, up to a constant,

$$
\ell(\boldsymbol{p},c,\phi)
=-\frac{G}{2}\log\phi
-\frac12\log\det\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})
-\frac{1}{2\phi}\,\boldsymbol{r}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{r}.
$$ {#eq-sc-loglik}

For a fixed composition both scales have closed forms, the generalised
least-squares coefficient of $\boldsymbol{y}$ on $\boldsymbol{m}$ and the mean
Mahalanobis residual:

$$
\hat c(\boldsymbol{p})
=\frac{\boldsymbol{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{y}}{\boldsymbol{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{m}},
\qquad
\hat\phi(\boldsymbol{p})=\frac{Q(\boldsymbol{p})}{G},
\qquad
Q(\boldsymbol{p})=\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\hat{\boldsymbol{r}} .
$$ {#eq-sc-closed-scales}

Substituting them leaves a function of the $J-1$ ILR coordinates,

$$
\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho})
=-\frac{G}{2}\log Q\bigl(\boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho})\bigr)
-\frac12\log\det\boldsymbol{S}_W\bigl(\boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho})\bigr)
+\text{const},
$$ {#eq-sc-profile}

[`profile_loglik_single_cell_ilr()`](../reference/profile_loglik_single_cell_ilr.html).
The weight matrix $\boldsymbol{W}$ depends on the unknown composition. The
profile rebuilds it, with $\hat c$ and $\hat\phi$, at every trial
composition, so the fit is a feasible generalised least squares without
an outer loop, and its maximiser is the joint maximum-likelihood
estimate of $(\boldsymbol{p},c,\phi)$. Alternating the closed-form scales
with a Newton fit in $\boldsymbol{p}$ reaches the same fixed point, but the
composition and the mean scale are coupled ($I_{pc}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$), so
that scheme converges only linearly.

## Profile score and Hessian {#sec-profile-derivatives}

By the envelope theorem the profile score needs no derivative of the
closed-form scales:

$$
\frac{\partial\ell^{\ast}}{\partial p_j}
=\frac{G}{Q}\Bigl(\hat c\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}
+\tfrac12\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}\boldsymbol{W}\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}\Bigr)
-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}).
$$ {#eq-sc-profile-score}

Differentiating once more, with $\boldsymbol{\eta}=(c,\phi)$ and
$\partial\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}/\partial\boldsymbol{p}^{\top}
=-\boldsymbol{H}_{\eta\eta}^{-1}\boldsymbol{H}_{\eta p}$, gives the Schur
complement of the observed Hessian of @eq-sc-loglik at the closed-form
scales. With $\boldsymbol{w}=\boldsymbol{W}\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla^{2}_{\boldsymbol{p}}\ell^{\ast}
&=\boldsymbol{H}_{pp}-\boldsymbol{H}_{p\eta}\boldsymbol{H}_{\eta\eta}^{-1}\boldsymbol{H}_{\eta p},\\
(\boldsymbol{H}_{pc})_{j}
&=\phi^{-1}\bigl(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}\boldsymbol{w}
-c\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{m}
-\boldsymbol{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}\boldsymbol{w}\bigr),\\
(\boldsymbol{H}_{p\phi})_{j}
&=-\phi^{-2}\bigl(c\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}\boldsymbol{w}
+\tfrac12\boldsymbol{w}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}\boldsymbol{w}\bigr),\\
H_{cc}&=-\boldsymbol{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{m}/\phi,
\qquad H_{c\phi}=0,
\qquad H_{\phi\phi}=-\frac{G}{2\phi^{2}} .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-sc-profile-hessian}

$H_{c\phi}=-\boldsymbol{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{w}/\phi^{2}$ and
$H_{\phi\phi}=G/(2\phi^{2})-\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{w}/\phi^{3}$
take these values only at $\hat c$ and $\hat\phi$. $\boldsymbol{H}_{pp}$ is
the Hessian in $\boldsymbol{p}$ at fixed scales. The ILR
[chain rule](theory-population-generative-optimisation.html#sec-chain-rule)
then adds the curvature of the chart. Score and Hessian
(`gradient_profile_loglik_single_cell_ilr()`,
`hessian_profile_loglik_single_cell_ilr()`) were checked against
Richardson-extrapolated numerical derivatives [@R-numDeriv] for three
and four cell types.

## Trust-region Newton {#sec-profile-trust-region}

Newton–Raphson maximises @eq-sc-profile with that score and Hessian,
safeguarded by the PORT trust region of `stats::nlminb()` [@R-base;
@gayAlgorithm611Subroutines1983], the driver of the population-level
fit. Each step maximises the quadratic model of $\ell^{\ast}$ inside a
ball of radius $\Delta$, $\boldsymbol{\delta}=(\lambda\mathbf{I}-\boldsymbol{H}_{\rho})^{-1}\boldsymbol{U}_{\rho}$
with the smallest $\lambda\ge0$ that makes the system positive definite
and keeps $\lVert\boldsymbol{\delta}\rVert\le\Delta$. The radius shrinks after a
poor prediction of the increase and grows after a good one. Fisher
scoring with step-halving is not used: the trust region already handles
an indefinite Hessian, and with $c^{2}/\phi=n$ cells the observed and
expected information nearly coincide at the maximum.

## Start and identifiability {#sec-profile-start}

The start solves
$\min_{c>0,\,\boldsymbol{p}\in\Delta^{J-1}}\lVert\boldsymbol{y}-c\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}\rVert_2^{2}$,
the quadratic programme of `DeconRNASeq`
[@gongDeconRNASeqStatisticalFramework2013] with a free scale
([`single_cell_nuisance_scales()`](../reference/single_cell_nuisance_scales.html)).
In the products $w_j=cp_j$ it is non-negative least squares, solved
exactly by enumerating the active sets ($J\le12$). Dividing by
$c^{(0)}=\mathbf{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{w}$ restores the sum-to-one constraint,
and $\boldsymbol{p}^{(0)}$ is floored away from zero. The equality
$\mathbf{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}=1$ can be imposed with $c$ fixed only when $c$
is known: with an unknown bulk scale, simplex least squares at $c=1$ is
misspecified, and the free-scale form is the matching baseline.

$\hat\phi>0$ needs residual degrees of freedom, so the fit requires
$G>J$. The maximum-likelihood divisor $G$ biases $\hat\phi$ downwards by
about $(G-J)/G$, so $\hat n=\hat c^{2}/\hat\phi$ is biased upwards; $\hat n$
and $\hat a=\hat\phi/\hat c$ are descriptors, not inputs of the fit. The
REML calibration of the intervals is in the
[single-cell inference vignette](theory-single-cell-inference.html#sec-sc-reml).
`profile = FALSE` keeps the scales at their start values. That
two-stage fit is not the joint maximum; it is kept for comparison, and
its variance needs the plug-in correction of @sec-plugin-uncertainty.

## L-BFGS-B on the closure chart {#sec-profile-lbfgsb}

`deconvolute_single_cell(optimiser = "lbfgsb")` maximises the same
profile log-likelihood on the closure chart
$\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{w}/\mathbf{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{w}$, $\boldsymbol{w}\ge\boldsymbol{0}$,
of the
[population vignette](theory-population-generative-optimisation.html#sec-closure-box).
The profile score @eq-sc-profile-score is mapped to $\boldsymbol{w}$ by the
closure gradient, and the scales stay concentrated out at every
iterate. Every KKT point of the box in $\boldsymbol{w}$ is a KKT point of
the simplex problem, so a type absent from the bulk is estimated at an
exact zero instead of being approached. At such an estimate the ILR
coordinates and the Wald covariances are undefined and returned as
`NA`; the profile interval and the boundary likelihood-ratio test remain
available. Newton–Raphson on ILR stays the default; both solvers return
the same estimate when the maximum is interior.
